newsitem.title: UK: Russian Urals eases, dismay greets Nigerian OSPs.
newsitem.headline: Russian Urals eases, dismay greets Nigerian OSPs.

text.p: Russian Urals remained under pressure from comfortable supply levels and meagre buying interest on Thursday after trading a touch lower on Wednesday, traders said.
A cargo of Urals loading May 27-29 changed hands at Dated Brent -$1.42, four cents adrift from the value achieved for a distressed parcel on Tuesday.
The value confirmed Wednesday's perception that values slipped from early buy/sell levels of Dated Brent -$1.25/-$1.15 to -$1.40/-$1.30.
"The result is that buyers are very relaxed," another trader said. "There is not much requirement and margins are poor, though not critical."
Traders were seeking information about the fate of a Urals offered on the water at around Dated Brent -$1.40.
One trader said there was talk that it had gone to a major European refiner at between Dated Brent -$1.45 and -$1.50.
But the refiner denied it and others said the cargo may have gone into an eastern Mediterranean destination by way of a European trader.
One trader said margins for a complex refinery in Spain and Italy had slid to around 50 to 60 cents a barrel on Wednesday, but could revive if cheaper Urals became established.
Margins have worsened due to the sudden rise in North Sea Brent, which has gained some $2.50 since the start of May and continues to keep buyers cautious.
About five or six Urals cargoes remained on offer for third decade May and early June.
But traders said talk of refinery cuts in the north was not echoed in the Mediterranean.
"There is not a consoldated trend," a trader said. "One day margins are positive, one day negative. The situation appears just under control for today."
Traders said they still had no word on the status of the loading on May 25 of a one million barrel cargo of Iraqi Kirkuk at the Turkish port of Ceyhan,
Some said there has been doubt about whether the loading, planned by Trafigura under a term contract with Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO), would be given final U.N. approval.
If crude prices remain firm the cargo could be at risk of deferral or cancellation if the revenues from the first 180-day period of the U.N. oil-for-food exchange overshoot the $2 billion target.

On Tuesday, diplomats on the U.N. sanctions committee on Iraq said everything appeared to be on track for an extension of the "oil-for-food" deal when the current period ends June 7. But they said the U.S.remained cagey about its position.

"Everyone is waiting for this decision," a trader said. "We assume there will be another programme. There might be a slightly delay in while details are sorted out but we expect cargoes to start appearing again after the 15th (of June)".
Reactions varying from disappointment to dismay greeted the new Nigerian Official Selling Price for June announced late on Tuesday, with many traders complaining the differentials were excessive.
"Nigerian numbers are not going to take the market higher on their own. It cannot change the market just like that," cautioned one trader.
Bonny Light was assessed variously at a premium in the mid-40 cents to 45-50 cents over Dated Brent, Brass River at a premium in the low 50s and Qua Iboe in the low to mid 40s.
Escravos was heard offered at a premium to Dated of the mid to high 30s and Forcados at a premium in the upper teens.
Traders said Far East demand looked insufficiently robust to hold up Nigerian values, although the higher OSPs might have a residual psychological effect on sellers' offers.
"But I think the Far East is pretty well done for the moment," said one trader.
-- William Maclean, London newsroom +44 171 542 7646
